title: Mourvèdre
description: Also called Monastrell in Spain and Mataro in Australia. A sun-loving grape of dark fruit, game and herbs.
L: Mourvèdre gives deep-coloured wines with blackberry and plum, plus savoury notes of game, leather, black pepper and the wild herbs of the Mediterranean garrigue. Tannins are high and firm; acidity is moderate. Young, it can be reductive and closed; with age, it opens into meaty, earthy complexity.

Mourvèdre comes from Spain, where it's called Monastrell, probably from the region of Valencia or Murcia. In France the name may come from Murviedro, near Valencia. In Australia and California it's often called Mataro, after the town of Mataró near Barcelona. It needs lots of heat and ripens very late.
Monastrell in Spain, Mataro in Australia
Match each name to where it's used.
One grape, three names, all pointing back to eastern Spain.

Look for deep colour, dark fruit with a gamey, meaty or herbal edge, and firm tannin. In blends, it adds structure and savouriness. A young Mourvèdre may smell slightly reductive, of struck match or rubber, which usually fades with air. It's often described as the head on its feet and tail in the sun, needing heat but some moisture.
Mourvèdre ripens early, so it suits cool climates.
Not true. It ripens very late and needs a hot, sunny climate.
Mourvèdre gives dark fruit, game and garrigue
It comes from Spain as Monastrell; Australia calls it Mataro
It needs heat and ripens very late

Spain has the most, mainly in Jumilla, Yecla, Alicante and Valencia, as Monastrell. In France, it's the star of Bandol in Provence and a partner in the southern Rhône and Languedoc. Australia grows it in the Barossa and McLaren Vale; California in Contra Costa and Paso Robles.

Mourvèdre is the M in GSM blends, with Grenache and Syrah. Grenache brings red fruit and alcohol, Syrah colour and spice, Mourvèdre tannin, dark fruit and a savoury frame that helps the blend age. In Châteauneuf-du-Pape, some estates use a high share, like Château de Beaucastel.
What does Mourvèdre bring to a GSM blend?
Mourvèdre adds structure and savoury depth; Grenache brings red fruit.

Mourvèdre needs a long, hot season, often harvested in October. It likes sea breezes and some water near the roots, which is why coastal Bandol suits it. It's drought-tolerant once established, and resists oxidation in winemaking. On its own roots in sandy soils, it survives in parts of Spain.
In cool, short seasons it won't ripen.
Spain grows the most, as Monastrell
Mourvèdre is the M in GSM, adding structure
It needs heat, a long season and likes the sea

Bandol lies on the Mediterranean coast of Provence, between Marseille and Toulon. Vineyards climb an amphitheatre of terraces, called restanques, facing south to the sea. Hot, sunny days and sea breezes ripen Mourvèdre fully. Limestone and sandy marl soils keep the vines healthy.

Bandol red must be at least 50% Mourvèdre, with Grenache and Cinsault, and age at least 18 months in oak before release. Most top producers use 75 to 95% Mourvèdre. The wines are dark, structured, gamey and herbal, and can age 20 years or more.
At least 50% Mourvèdre, 18 months in oak
Bandol red must age at least ____ months in oak.
Eighteen months in wood softens Mourvèdre's firm tannins.

Bandol's rosé is among Provence's most serious: more structured than most, often with Mourvèdre at its core, and able to age a few years. The small amount of white wine uses Clairette, Ugni Blanc and Bourboulenc. Domaine Tempier, a family estate, helped define Bandol's modern reputation.
Bandol rosé is often more structured than typical Provence rosé.
Yes. Mourvèdre gives it more body and ageing potential.
Bandol's terraces face the sea, ripening Mourvèdre fully
Reds need at least 50% Mourvèdre and 18 months in oak
Bandol rosé is structured and can age
Explain how heat and drought shape it

In Spain, Monastrell dominates the hot, dry south-east. Jumilla, Yecla and Alicante are its main DOs. Vineyards sit at 400 to 800 m on poor, limestone soils, often as old bush vines, many ungrafted because phylloxera struggles in sandy soils. Rainfall is low, often 300 mm a year.
Old bush vines in the dry south-east

The heat gives ripe, dark fruit and high alcohol, often 14.5 to 15.5%. Drought keeps berries small and concentrated. Altitude brings cooler nights, preserving some freshness. Once known for bulk wines, these regions now make concentrated reds at good prices, and some powerful, oaked premium wines.
Why are many Monastrell vines in south-east Spain ungrafted?
Sandy soils make it hard for phylloxera to move, so some old vines grow on their own roots.

Alicante also makes Fondillón, a historic sweet wine from overripe Monastrell, fermented naturally and aged for at least 10 years in old casks, often in a solera. It reaches 16 to 18% alcohol without fortification. It was famous in the 17th and 18th centuries and is now a protected rarity.
Match each Spanish term to its meaning.
South-east Spain is Monastrell's home ground.
Jumilla, Yecla and Alicante are Monastrell's heartland
Heat and drought give ripe, dark, powerful reds
Fondillón is Alicante's historic aged sweet wine

Mourvèdre's gamey, herbal style suits Provençal and Mediterranean food: lamb with rosemary, beef daube, game, wild boar, grilled sausages. Bandol rosé is a classic with bouillabaisse, Marseille's fish stew. Spanish Monastrell suits roast lamb, chorizo and hearty stews.

Serve reds at 16 to 18 degrees. Young Bandol can be closed and reductive; decant it for an hour or two. Good Bandol ages 15 to 25 years, gaining leather, truffle and dried herbs. Most Spanish Monastrell is best within five years; premium examples age longer.
Which dish is a classic partner for Bandol rosé?
Bandol rosé's structure suits the rich, saffron-scented fish stew of Marseille.
If a young Mourvèdre smells of struck match, give it time in a decanter. That reductive note usually fades, revealing fruit and herbs.
Good Bandol red can age for 15 to 25 years.
Yes. Mourvèdre's tannin and resistance to oxidation help it age.
Mourvèdre suits lamb, game and Provençal dishes
Decant young Bandol; serve at 16 to 18 degrees
Match each name or place to Mourvèdre.
One grape with many names and homes.
At least 50% Mourvèdre, and top producers use much more.
Mourvèdre ripens early and suits cool regions.
Not true. It needs heat and ripens very late.
Which aromas are typical of Mourvèdre?
Passion fruit belongs to Sauvignon Blanc.
In GSM blends, the M stands for ____.
Mourvèdre is dark, gamey, herbal and firm
It's Monastrell in Spain and Mataro in Australia
Bandol is its finest French expression
It loves heat and suits Mediterranean food
